items.label: text
items.text: We will use this chart to analyse the two spectra for propanol.

items.label: text
items.text: In the spectrum of propan-1-ol the peaks appear at 65, 25 and 10 ppm. The only relevant ranges in the chart are C—C (the range is approximately 60-0 ppm) and C—OH (the range is approximately 75-55 ppm).

items.label: text
items.text: This means that the peak at 65 ppm corresponds to C—OH, so this is the carbon in the CH2OH group. The peaks at 25 and 10 ppm correspond to C—C, so these are the carbons in the CH; and CH2 groups.Notice that it is not possible to decide whether the peak at 25 ppm is due to the CH or the CH2 group.

items.label: text
items.text: In the spectrum of propan-2-ol the peaks appear at 65 and 27 ppm. The only relevant ranges in the chart are again C—C and C—OH.

items.label: text
items.text: This means that the peak at 65 ppm corresponds to C—OH, so this is the carbon in the CHOH group. The peak at 27 ppm corresponds to C—C, so this is due to the carbons in the two CH3 groups. The peak at 27 ppm is bigger than the one at 65 ppm because it is caused by two carbon atoms, not one.

items.label: text
items.text: Fig C shows theinterpretation of these twospectra.
